summary: RISC and CISC processor architectures — what an instruction set is, opcodes, operands and clock cycles, the characteristics of RISC (simple fixed-length instructions, load/store, many registers, hard-wired control, pipelining) and of CISC (complex variable-length instructions, memory operands, microcode), the same task on both, the performance equation, and a full comparison with uses, advantages, disadvantages and exam-style answers.

blocks.content: Every program that runs on a computer — a web browser, a game, the operating system itself — is finally carried out by the **processor (CPU)** as a long sequence of very small steps called **machine-code instructions**. A processor cannot understand Python, Java or C++. It only understands its own fixed list of binary instructions, such as "load a value from memory", "add two numbers", "store a result", "compare two values" and "jump to another instruction". A compiler or interpreter translates the programmer's code into these instructions.

The designers of a processor must decide **which instructions** it will understand, **how complex** each instruction is, **how long** each one is in bits, **where** the data for each instruction can come from (registers or memory), and **how** the control unit will carry each one out. Together these design decisions are called the processor's **architecture** (more precisely, its **instruction set architecture**, ISA). There are two main approaches: **RISC** and **CISC**.

A single **binary command** that the processor can decode and execute directly. It is made of an **opcode**, which says **what operation** to perform (for example ADD or LOAD), and usually one or more **operands**, which give the **data**, the **register** or the **memory address** to use.

The **complete set of machine-code instructions** that a particular processor can decode and execute. Programs compiled for one instruction set **cannot run directly** on a processor with a different instruction set.

An instruction is stored in memory as a binary pattern, just like data. Part of the pattern is the **opcode**; the remaining bits hold the **operands**. For example, an instruction meaning "ADD R1, R2, R3" (add the contents of registers R2 and R3 and put the result in R1) might be stored as a 32-bit word: some bits for the opcode ADD, and a few bits for each register number. An instruction such as "LOAD R1, 2048" needs bits for an address instead.

How these bits are laid out is called the **instruction format**. In some processors **every instruction has the same length** (for example exactly 32 bits) and the fields are always in the same places. In others, instructions have **different lengths** — a short instruction might be 1 byte and a long one 15 bytes — depending on how many operands it has and what kind they are. As you will see, this one choice has a big effect on how fast and how simply the processor can **decode** instructions.

blocks.text: Clock cycles and cycles per instruction

blocks.content: The processor is driven by a **clock** that sends out pulses at a fixed rate. Each pulse is one **clock cycle**. A 3 GHz processor has 3 000 000 000 cycles every second, so one cycle lasts about a third of a nanosecond. Each instruction takes a certain number of clock cycles to be fetched, decoded and executed. The average number of cycles an instruction needs is called **CPI — cycles per instruction**.

One "tick" of the processor's clock — the smallest unit of time in which the CPU does a step of work. The **clock speed** (for example 3 GHz = 3 × 10⁹ cycles per second) is the number of cycles per second. An instruction takes **one or more** clock cycles.
The time a program takes depends on three things, and this gives the most useful idea for understanding RISC and CISC:

blocks.latex: \text{time for a program} = \text{number of instructions} \times \text{cycles per instruction (CPI)} \times \text{time per cycle}
blocks.caption: The performance equation

blocks.content: A designer can make a program faster by reducing **any** of the three factors. The **CISC** approach tries to reduce the **number of instructions** in a program: if one powerful instruction can do the work of four simple ones, the program is shorter. The **RISC** approach tries to reduce the **cycles per instruction**: if every instruction is so simple that it finishes in one cycle (and the processor can overlap instructions), the program runs quickly even though it contains more instructions. Both approaches can also raise the clock speed, but simpler circuits make that easier for RISC.

blocks.text: The control unit: hard-wired or microprogrammed

blocks.content: The **control unit** decodes each instruction and sends control signals to the other parts of the CPU (the ALU, registers, buses) to carry it out. There are two ways of building it. A **hard-wired** control unit uses fixed logic circuits: each opcode directly switches on the right signals. This is very fast but only practical when the instructions are few and simple. A **microprogrammed** control unit stores, inside the CPU, a small program of **micro-instructions (microcode)** for each machine-code instruction; executing one complex instruction means running its little microprogram step by step. This makes it possible to have hundreds of complex instructions, but each one takes several cycles.

A set of **micro-instructions stored inside the CPU's control unit**. Each complex machine-code instruction is carried out by running its own short sequence of micro-instructions. Used in **CISC** processors; RISC processors usually have a **hard-wired** control unit made of fixed logic circuits.

blocks.title: Hard-wired and microprogrammed control units
rows: Fixed logic circuits turn each opcode directly into control signals
Each instruction runs a stored sequence of micro-instructions (microcode)
Number / complexity of instructions it suits
Hard — the circuit must be redesigned
Easier — the microcode can be changed (even updated after manufacture)

blocks.content: The RISC idea came from research in the late 1970s and early 1980s (IBM, and university projects at Berkeley and Stanford). Researchers measured real programs and found that compilers used a **small number of simple instructions** most of the time; the many complex instructions of the processors of that time were **rarely used**, yet they made the chips complicated and slow. Their conclusion was to build processors with **only simple instructions**, make each of them **very fast**, and let the **compiler** combine them to do complex work.

A processor architecture with a **small set of simple instructions**, each of the **same (fixed) length**, most of which execute in **one clock cycle**. Only **LOAD** and **STORE** instructions access main memory; all other operations use the processor's **many registers**. Complex tasks are built from **several simple instructions**, so the emphasis is on **software** (the compiler).
Each characteristic below is a possible mark in a "describe" question. Learn **what** it is and **why** RISC has it.

items.title: A small set of simple instructions
items.content: A RISC processor has a **reduced** number of instructions (often fewer than a hundred basic ones), and each does **one simple job**: add two registers, load one value, compare, branch. Because each instruction is simple, the circuits to carry it out are small and fast.

items.title: One instruction per clock cycle
items.content: Most RISC instructions are designed to finish their execution in **one clock cycle**, so the CPI is close to 1. This makes the time each instruction takes **predictable**, which is exactly what a pipeline needs.

items.title: Fixed-length instructions
items.content: Every instruction is the **same size** (for example 32 bits) with the opcode and register numbers always in the same bit positions. The decoder never has to work out where an instruction ends, so decoding is **simple and fast**, and the next instruction can be fetched straight away.

items.title: Load/store architecture
items.content: Only two kinds of instruction — **LOAD** (memory → register) and **STORE** (register → memory) — can access main memory. Arithmetic and logic work **only on registers**. This keeps every other instruction short and quick, because accessing memory is slow compared with accessing a register.

items.title: Many general-purpose registers
items.content: Since all calculations take place in registers, RISC processors provide **many** of them — typically **32** (MIPS, RISC-V; 64-bit ARM has 31). Values can stay inside the CPU instead of being written to and read from memory again and again.

items.title: Few, simple addressing modes
items.content: An addressing mode is the way an instruction says where its data is (a constant, a register, an address). RISC offers only **a few simple modes**, again keeping decoding fast and circuits small.

items.title: Hard-wired control unit, fewer transistors
items.content: Simple instructions can be decoded by **fixed logic circuits** instead of microcode. The chip needs **fewer transistors** for control, so it is **smaller, cheaper**, uses **less power** and produces **less heat**. The space saved on the chip can be used for more registers or cache.

items.title: More work for the compiler
items.content: Because there are no complex instructions, a program needs **more instructions** and its machine code is **longer**, taking **more memory (RAM)**. The **compiler** must be clever: it chooses the simple instructions, keeps values in registers and orders instructions so that the pipeline is never kept waiting.

blocks.content: The biggest advantage of RISC's simple, equal-sized, one-cycle instructions is that they are ideal for **pipelining**. Every instruction goes through the same stages — **fetch**, **decode**, **execute** (real processors split these into more stages, such as memory access and write-back). Without a pipeline the CPU finishes one instruction completely before starting the next, so most of its circuits are idle most of the time. With a pipeline, as soon as an instruction moves from the fetch stage to the decode stage, the **next instruction is fetched**, just as on a factory assembly line several cars are being built at once, each at a different station.

A technique in which the processor works on **several instructions at the same time**, each at a **different stage** of the fetch–decode–execute cycle: while one instruction is being executed, the next is being decoded and the one after that is being fetched. Once the pipeline is full, **one instruction is completed every clock cycle**.

blocks.caption: A three-stage pipeline: after it fills, one instruction finishes every cycle

blocks.content: For **n** instructions in a pipeline with **k** stages (each taking one cycle), the first instruction needs **k** cycles to come out of the end, and after that one more instruction finishes **every cycle**:

For 100 instructions in a 3-stage pipeline that is 300 cycles without pipelining and only 102 with it — almost three times faster. This works smoothly only if every stage takes the **same time**, which is why RISC's fixed-length, one-cycle instructions matter so much. A pipeline can still be slowed down: if an instruction needs the result of the instruction just before it, or if a **branch** (jump) means the instructions already fetched are the wrong ones, the pipeline must wait or be emptied ("flushed").

blocks.title: Examples of RISC processors and where they are used
blocks.content: **ARM** processors are in almost every **smartphone and tablet**, in the **Raspberry Pi**, smart watches, smart TVs and many **embedded systems** (washing machines, cars, routers). **Apple M-series** chips in MacBooks and iPads are ARM-based. Other RISC families: **RISC-V** (an open, royalty-free design growing fast in IoT devices), **MIPS**, **PowerPC**. Many of the world's fastest supercomputers also use RISC (ARM) processors.

CISC is the older approach. In the 1960s and 1970s **memory was very expensive and slow**, and much software was written directly in **assembly language** by hand, while compilers were simple. Designers therefore tried to make each instruction do **as much work as possible**: a program with fewer, more powerful instructions took up **less memory**, needed **fewer slow fetches from memory**, and was easier for a programmer to write. Over time more and more specialised instructions were added — for string copying, loops, decimal arithmetic and so on. The name "CISC" was only invented later, to contrast these designs with RISC.

A processor architecture with a **large set of complex instructions** of **variable length**. A **single instruction** can carry out **several low-level operations** — for example load a value from memory, perform a calculation and store the result — and may take **several clock cycles**. Instructions can work **directly on data in memory**, and the emphasis is on **hardware**.

items.title: A large set of complex instructions
items.content: A CISC processor has **hundreds** of instructions (modern x86 has well over a thousand variants), including very specialised ones such as "copy a whole block of memory", "repeat until a counter reaches zero" or "multiply two values from memory". One instruction may do the work of several RISC instructions.

items.title: Multi-cycle instructions
items.content: Complex instructions need **several clock cycles** — and **different** instructions need **different numbers** of cycles (a register addition may take 1, a division or a memory-to-memory operation many more). The CPI is greater than 1 and not predictable.

items.title: Variable-length instructions
items.content: Instructions have **different sizes** (in x86, from 1 to 15 bytes) depending on the operation and its operands. Short instructions save memory, but the decoder must examine the first bytes of each instruction to find out **how long** it is before it can find the next one, which makes decoding **slower and more complex**.

items.title: Memory operands (memory-to-memory operations)
items.content: Many CISC instructions can use data **directly in main memory**: one instruction can read a value from memory, change it and write it back. There is no need to load everything into registers first, so CISC processors traditionally have **fewer general-purpose registers** (early x86 had 8; x86-64 has 16).

items.title: Many addressing modes
items.content: CISC offers **many ways** to specify an operand — a constant, a register, a memory address, an address held in a register, an address plus an offset, an address plus an index × a scale… This gives the programmer flexibility but makes instructions longer and decoding more complex.

items.title: Microprogrammed control unit, more transistors
items.content: Complex instructions are carried out by **microcode** stored in the control unit. The decoding and control circuits need **many more transistors**, so the chip is **larger, more expensive**, uses **more power** and produces **more heat** — desktop CPUs need heat sinks and fans.

items.title: Shorter programs, simpler compilers
items.content: Because each instruction does more, programs contain **fewer instructions**, so the machine code is **shorter** and needs **less RAM**. Translating a high-level statement into one complex instruction is easier, so the **compiler** has less work to do, and assembly language is easier to write by hand.

blocks.title: Examples of CISC processors and where they are used
blocks.content: **Intel x86 / x86-64** (Core i3/i5/i7/i9, Xeon) and **AMD** (Ryzen, EPYC) processors in most **desktop PCs, laptops and servers**, and in games consoles such as the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X. Older examples: Intel 8086, Motorola 68000, VAX. A huge amount of existing software (Windows programs, games) is compiled for x86, which is one important reason CISC is still used: **backward compatibility**.

blocks.text: Modern CISC processors work like RISC inside

blocks.content: Today the difference between the two is less sharp than it used to be. Since the mid-1990s, Intel and AMD processors have **translated** each complex x86 instruction, as it is decoded, into one or more simple, fixed-size **micro-operations** — effectively RISC-like instructions — which are then executed by a fast, deeply **pipelined** core. The processor still accepts the CISC instruction set, so old software runs unchanged, but internally it gets many of RISC's speed advantages. At the same time, RISC instruction sets have gradually added some more powerful instructions (for example for multimedia and encryption). The cost for CISC is the extra translation hardware, which uses chip space and power — one reason why ARM processors are more energy-efficient in phones and laptops.
The clearest way to see the difference is to give both architectures **the same job**.
The task: **multiply** the two numbers stored in memory locations **2:3** and **5:2** and **store** the result back in **2:3**. On a **CISC** processor one instruction does everything:
MULT 2:3, 5:2        ; load both values, multiply them, store the result in 2:3
blocks.caption: CISC — one complex instruction (several clock cycles)

blocks.content: On a **RISC** processor the same job needs four simple instructions, because only LOAD and STORE may touch memory and the multiplication works on registers:

LOAD  A, 2:3         ; copy the first value from memory into register A
LOAD  B, 5:2         ; copy the second value into register B
PROD  A, B           ; multiply registers A and B, result in A
STORE 2:3, A         ; copy the result from A back to memory
blocks.caption: RISC — four simple instructions (about one clock cycle each)

blocks.title: Worked example 1 — what the two programs show
blocks.content:
- **Length of the program.** The CISC program is **one** instruction long, the RISC program **four**. So the CISC code needs **less memory**, and the RISC code needs **more RAM** and a compiler that generates more instructions.
- **Cycles per instruction.** The CISC instruction must load two values, multiply and store, so it takes **several clock cycles** and needs complex circuits (microcode). Each RISC instruction is simple and takes about **one cycle**, and the four instructions can flow through a **pipeline**.
- **Who does the work.** In CISC the **hardware** does the work of splitting the job into steps; in RISC the **software** (the compiler) does it by producing four instructions.
- **Total time.** The total time can be similar — CISC has fewer instructions but more cycles each; RISC has more instructions but fewer cycles each. The work has moved from **hardware** (CISC) to **software** (RISC).

blocks.title: Worked example 2 — using the performance equation
blocks.content:
A program is compiled for two processors, both running at **2 GHz** (one cycle = 0.5 ns).
- **CISC** version: **1 000 000** instructions, average **CPI = 4**. Time = 1 000 000 × 4 × 0.5 ns = 2 000 000 ns = **2 ms**.
- **RISC** version: the compiler needs **1 500 000** instructions (50 % more), but with pipelining the average **CPI = 1.2**. Time = 1 500 000 × 1.2 × 0.5 ns = 900 000 ns = **0.9 ms**.

The RISC program has **more instructions** but finishes in **less than half the time**, because each instruction takes far fewer cycles. If the RISC CPI rose to 3 (for example because branches kept emptying the pipeline), its time would be 1 500 000 × 3 × 0.5 ns = 2.25 ms — slower than CISC. Neither design is "always faster": it depends on the number of instructions **and** the cycles per instruction.

blocks.title: Advantages and disadvantages of each architecture
rows: Each instruction executes **quickly** (about one cycle) · **pipelining** is simple and efficient · simple hard-wired circuits → **low power and heat**, long battery life, no fan · **smaller, cheaper** chips · spare chip area for more registers / cache

**Fewer instructions** per program → **shorter code**, less RAM · **simpler compilers** and easier assembly programming · one instruction can do a complex job such as copying a block of memory · **backward compatible** with decades of x86 software

Programs need **more instructions** → longer code, **more RAM** · **more work for the compiler** (and for anyone writing assembly) · performance depends heavily on a good compiler · software compiled for x86 must be recompiled or emulated

Complex instructions take **several cycles** · variable length makes decoding and **pipelining harder** · **more transistors → more power, more heat, higher cost** · many complex instructions are **rarely used**, wasting chip area

blocks.text: Why phones use RISC and desktop PCs use CISC

blocks.content: This is a typical "explain" question, and the answer comes from the characteristics above. A **smartphone** runs on a **battery** and has **no fan**, so the most important requirement is **low power consumption and little heat**. A RISC processor such as ARM has simple, hard-wired circuits with **fewer transistors**, so it uses less power and produces less heat, giving **longer battery life** in a thin case; it is also **cheaper and smaller**, which matters in a device made in hundreds of millions. A **desktop PC** is plugged into the mains and has room for a heat sink and fan, so power matters less; what matters is running the huge range of existing **Windows software and games compiled for x86**, so CISC processors from Intel and AMD remain the standard there. The line is moving, though: Apple moved its Mac computers to ARM (RISC) chips in 2020 because they gave high performance with much lower power use, and ARM processors are increasingly used in servers to save electricity in data centres.

- Saying RISC is "slower because it has fewer instructions". Each RISC instruction is **faster**; overall speed depends on the number of instructions **and** the cycles per instruction.
- Saying CISC has **more registers**. RISC has **more** registers, because all its calculations use registers; CISC can work directly on memory.
- Mixing up the **number of instructions in the instruction set** (RISC has **fewer**) with the **number of instructions in a program** (RISC needs **more**).
- Writing one-sided "comparisons" ("RISC uses one clock cycle"). Each point must cover **both**: "RISC instructions usually take one clock cycle, **whereas** CISC instructions may take several".
- Saying CISC programs use **more** memory. CISC programs are **shorter**, so they use **less** memory for code.
- Saying RISC means "no complex tasks are possible". RISC can do any task — it builds complex operations from **several simple instructions**.

blocks.title: Exam-style questions with model answers
blocks.content:
**Q: State what is meant by the instruction set of a processor. [1]**
The complete set of machine-code instructions that the processor can decode and execute (1).

**Q: Describe the RISC architecture. [4]**
RISC uses a small set of simple instructions (1) of fixed length (1) that each execute in about one clock cycle (1); only LOAD/STORE instructions access memory and it has many general-purpose registers (1); it is well suited to pipelining / has a hard-wired control unit (1). (Max 4.)

**Q: Describe the CISC architecture. [3]**
CISC has a large set of complex instructions (1); one instruction can carry out several low-level operations, e.g. load, calculate and store, and take several clock cycles (1); instructions are of variable length and can operate directly on data in memory / use a microprogrammed control unit (1).

**Q: Compare RISC and CISC. [4]**
RISC has a small set of simple instructions, whereas CISC has a large set of complex instructions (1). RISC instructions are fixed length and take one cycle, whereas CISC instructions are variable length and take several cycles (1). RISC programs need more instructions / more RAM, whereas CISC programs are shorter (1). RISC uses less power and produces less heat, whereas CISC uses more power because it has more transistors (1).

**Q: Explain why most smartphones use RISC processors. [2]**
RISC processors have simpler circuits / fewer transistors (1), so they use less power and produce less heat, giving longer battery life without a fan (1).

**Q: A 4-stage pipeline executes 20 instructions, each stage taking one clock cycle. Calculate the number of cycles needed with and without pipelining. [2]**
Without: 20 × 4 = **80 cycles** (1). With: 4 + (20 − 1) = **23 cycles** (1).

- Listing features with no explanation in a "describe" or "explain" question. Add **why**: "fixed-length instructions, **so** they are quick to decode".
- Giving examples without the architecture: "ARM" earns a mark only when linked to RISC ("ARM is a RISC processor used in smartphones").
- In pipeline calculations, writing n + k instead of k + (n − 1).
